manual.simpleradio.start.title: Getting started
manual.simpleradio.start.text:
# Welcome to amateur radio
This mod turns Simple Radio into a small ham radio world: handhelds, stations, repeaters, antennas, propagation, licences and digital modes.
# First steps
* Take the licence exam (booklet item) to get your own call sign. It is optional: no licence is needed to transmit.
* Get a handheld transceiver. Sneak + use opens its settings; hold use to talk.
* Build a station with an antenna and a 13.8 V power supply for long distance.
* Signals are weakened by hills, buildings, caves and distance. Go high for VHF/UHF, use HF for long distance.
# Receiving is always free
Every radio can listen on every frequency. Only the band plan limits where you transmit.
Use the chapters on the left; scroll with the mouse wheel or the arrow keys.
manual.simpleradio.licence.title: Licence and bands
manual.simpleradio.licence.text:
# No licence needed
Anyone may transmit on the amateur bands. The licence is optional: it gives you a call sign. (A server can make it compulsory with band_plan.requireLicense.)
# The licence exam
Use the licence exam booklet. You get 10 questions; 7 correct answers pass. If you fail you can try again after 5 minutes. The questions are about everything in this manual.
# Call signs
Passing gives you a call sign like TA3KQ. APRS sends it (otherwise your name) and stations show it as the operator. /telsiz lisans shows yours.
# Band plan
Amateur radios (handheld, station, mobile, APRS) transmit only on the amateur bands:
* HF: 160 m 1.810-2.000, 80 m 3.500-3.800, 40 m 7.000-7.200, 30 m 10.100-10.150, 20 m 14.000-14.350, 17 m 18.068-18.168, 15 m 21.000-21.450, 12 m 24.890-24.990, 10 m 28.000-29.700 MHz
* VHF: 6 m 50-52, 2 m 144-146 MHz
* UHF: 70 cm 430-440 MHz
# PMR446
Walkie talkies are licence free PMR446 radios with 16 channels from 446.00625 MHz, 12.5 kHz apart. They cannot leave those channels.
manual.simpleradio.handheld.title: Handhelds
manual.simpleradio.handheld.text:
# Talking
Hold use to transmit, release to listen. A handheld does not hear while it transmits (half duplex).
# Settings (sneak + use)
* Receive frequency, FM/AM/SSB, shift for repeaters (simplex, ±0.6, ±7.6 MHz) and on/off.
* CTCSS: a transmit tone and a receive tone squelch. With a receive tone set, you only hear stations sending that tone.
# Memory channels
16 stored channels with names. Store, Recall and Delete them in the settings screen. PageUp / PageDown step through them while holding the radio.
# Dual watch and scan
Dual watch listens to a second frequency too; the main one has priority and you always transmit on it. Scan steps through the stored channels (at least 2), 10 a second, and stops on a busy channel.
# Battery
A full battery lasts 4 Minecraft days of listening; transmitting drains it 4 times faster. Under half charge the output drops; under 10% it beeps. Charge it in the charging station, or craft the radio with a charged battery pack to swap packs.
# Display
The overlay next to the hotbar shows frequency, channel, S-meter, TX, battery and scan state.
manual.simpleradio.station.title: Station
manual.simpleradio.station.text:
# The station
A base station for HF, VHF and UHF with 1-100 W output. Right-click opens its front panel: bands, frequency, mode (FM/AM/SSB), shift, power, CTCSS tones, RIT and VOX.
# Talking
* Hold B (station push-to-talk) within about 4 blocks.
* Desk microphone: place it within 4 blocks of the station; look at it and hold use (up to 6 blocks away).
* Hand microphone: use it on a station to link it, then hold use anywhere within about 8 blocks.
* VOX: with VOX on, simply talking near the station keys it.
# SSB and RIT
Single sideband gets through where FM is lost in the noise. If the other station is a little off frequency the voice sounds too high or too low: turn the RIT (clarifier, ±990 Hz) until it sounds right.
# S-meter
The panel shows the strength of the received signal in S units (one S unit is 4 dB) and the noise from nearby machines (QRM). Looking at an original radio or receiver block shows its S-meter next to the crosshair, or why it is silent (no power, no catalyst).
# Heat
The power amplifier warms up while transmitting, much faster into a bad antenna. At 100% it shuts off until it cools to 60%.
# Scanner
The scanner block sweeps from a start to an end frequency in steps of 5-100 kHz, 200 channels a second, and stops on a signal. Skip leaves a busy channel alone for a while.
manual.simpleradio.antennas.title: Antennas and SWR
manual.simpleradio.antennas.text:
# Antennas
Stack antenna mast blocks on top of the station; a yagi on top makes it directional. A dual band vertical can be connected with coax cable from further away.
* Mast: fine on VHF/UHF; on HF it needs to be near a quarter wave long (e.g. about 5 blocks on 14 MHz, 10 on 7 MHz).
* Yagi: about 12 dBi forward and weak behind. Use it or the station panel to turn it.
* Without any antenna the station radiates almost nothing.
# SWR
A badly matched antenna reflects power back: the panel shows a high SWR, the station turns its power down, loses signal and heats up quickly.
# Antenna tuner
Place an antenna tuner touching the station. It matches antennas up to SWR 10 down to 1.1, so a short mast works on HF too (a little less efficiently).
# Height
Antennas high above the ground reach further on VHF/UHF (radio horizon) and hear over hills.
manual.simpleradio.power.title: Power
manual.simpleradio.power.text:
# 13.8 V DC
Stations, repeaters, scanners and fox transmitters run on 13.8 V DC. With Electrodynamics, mains fed straight into them is refused, and a voltage far above mains makes them explode. Forge Energy (FE) has no voltage: FE can power them directly.
# Power supply
Place the 13.8 V power supply by clicking a face of the radio: its DC output faces the radio. Feed mains (or FE) into any other side. The meters light up while it delivers power.
# A 13.8 V line
The output can also feed an Electrodynamics wire: everything on that wire gets 13.8 V, so one supply can run a whole shack (stations, repeaters, scanners, foxes, chargers and the original radio blocks).
# Consumption
Receiving uses little. Transmitting uses the output power divided by the amplifier efficiency, so 100 W is hungry.
# Original blocks
The original Simple Radio blocks (radio, transmitter, receiver, speaker) and the charger also need electricity unless the server turns it off. They run on mains or on the 13.8 V line.
manual.simpleradio.repeater.title: Repeaters
manual.simpleradio.repeater.text:
# How a repeater works
It listens on its input (output + shift) and sends everything it hears again on its output, with its own power and antenna. Example: output 438.650, shift -7.600: handhelds set RX 438.650 and shift -7.6.
# Settings
* Access tone: a CTCSS tone users must send to open the repeater. It can also send its own output tone.
* Time-out: a single transmission is cut after 180 seconds (a "bonk" tone).
* Call sign: the repeater identifies itself in morse every 10 minutes of activity, at the end of a transmission.
* Link: repeaters with the same link number (1-9999) pass their traffic to each other.
# Location
A repeater keeps its chunks loaded while it is on, so it works when nobody is near. Put it high with a mast.
manual.simpleradio.propagation.title: Propagation
manual.simpleradio.propagation.text:
# VHF and UHF: line of sight
* Hills and mountains between two stations weaken or block the signal; a signal just grazing a ridge loses a little, one deep behind a mountain a lot.
* Beyond the radio horizon (it grows with the square root of antenna height) the signal fades quickly. Go high.
* Inside buildings, under roofs and especially underground and in caves signals are weak. Blocks above the antenna cost signal; open sky helps.
# HF: ground wave and sky wave
* The ground wave covers a limited distance, less on the higher bands.
* The sky wave bounces off the ionosphere: very far, but with a skip zone around the station where nothing arrives.
* Low bands (80 m, 40 m) are best at night; high bands (15 m, 10 m) open by day and when solar flux is high.
* Solar flux changes over a 27 day cycle; magnetic storms raise the K index and close the high bands. Sporadic E sometimes opens 6 m and 10 m.
* /telsiz yayilim shows today's conditions.
# FM capture and interference
On FM the stronger of two stations takes over; similar signals sound garbled. Receivers tuned slightly off hear a weaker, distorted signal.
manual.simpleradio.weather.title: Weather and noise
manual.simpleradio.weather.text:
# Thunderstorms
* Storms add static crashes on HF.
* Antennas at least 6 blocks high attract lightning during thunder, taller ones more often.
* A lightning rod within 3 blocks of the antenna top takes the strike. A lightning rod touching the radio grounds it.
* An unprotected station, repeater or scanner burns out. Repair it by using it with 4 redstone.
# Man-made noise (QRM)
Running electric machines (anything using FE or Electrodynamics power while working) near a receiver raise its noise floor. The station panel shows it as QRM. Keep your shack away from the factory.
manual.simpleradio.fox.title: Fox hunting
manual.simpleradio.fox.text:
# Fox transmitter
A small beacon that sends its identity in morse (MOE, MOI, MOS, MOH, MO5) and a long tone. Use it with an empty hand to choose the fox number (1-5), or with a handheld to copy the handheld's frequency (default 144.500 MHz). With a hunt cycle set on the server, the foxes take turns.
# Direction finder
A receiver with a small yagi: it hears best in the direction you look. Turn around, find where the signal is strongest and walk there.
* Use: steps the attenuator (0/10/20/30 dB). Close to the fox, attenuate so the peak is still sharp.
* Sneak + use: frequency settings.
manual.simpleradio.aprs.title: APRS
manual.simpleradio.aprs.text:
# Automatic position reports
The APRS handheld is a normal transceiver that also sends your position on 144.800 MHz every 90 seconds (every 20 seconds when moving fast). The packets are real 1200 baud AX.25: a real APRS decoder listening to the speaker can read them.
* It sends your call sign (or your name without a licence) with -7.
* Sneak + use, then APRS: a map of the stations heard in the last 30 minutes (with zoom), a beacon switch and your comment.
* Only packets that arrive clearly enough are decoded.
manual.simpleradio.sstv.title: SSTV pictures
manual.simpleradio.sstv.text:
# Slow scan television
The SSTV terminal sends a map as a picture over the radio, in the real Robot 36 mode (about 37 seconds).
* Place it within 2 blocks of a station; the station's frequency and antenna are used.
* Put a filled map in the TX slot and press Send picture.
* On the receiving side, keep blank maps in the MAP slot: the picture is printed onto a locked map in the RX slot.
* The screen shows the picture line by line as it comes in. A weak signal gives a snowy picture; if the signal is lost the part received so far is printed.
manual.simpleradio.mobile.title: Mobile radio
manual.simpleradio.mobile.text:
# In a vehicle
The mobile radio works like a handheld, but while you ride anything - a boat, a minecart, a horse, a Create seat or an aircraft - it runs from the vehicle at 25 W with an antenna on the roof, and charges its battery.
* The cabin does not shield the roof antenna, but tunnels and caves still do.
* Carried by hand it is a 5 W handheld on its battery.
* Hold use to talk, sneak + use for the settings, like any handheld.
manual.simpleradio.commands.title: Commands
manual.simpleradio.commands.text:
# For everyone
* /telsiz lisans - your licence and call sign
* /telsiz yayilim - solar flux, K index, MUF, sporadic E and the state of the HF bands
# For operators
* /telsiz lisans ver <player> - grant a licence
* /telsiz lisans iptal <player> - revoke a licence
* /telsiz cagri <player> <call sign> - set a call sign
# Keys
* B - station push-to-talk (microphones: look at them / hold use)
* PageUp / PageDown - handheld channel up / down
The server's rules (battery, band plan, power) are sent to your client when you join.
